A1.justification: Both PDFs concern the LayerT2V research project, although v2 substantially redesigns its method and scope. All pages, including equations, tables, figures, and appendices, are readable and support comparison. The changed experimental settings limit direct performance comparisons, not document comparability.

before.justification: V1 reports original trajectory-control experiments, quantitative baseline comparisons, component ablations, and user preferences in Section 4 and Appendix C.

after.justification: V2 reports original VidLayer dataset statistics, generation experiments, VBench comparisons, ablations, user-study results, and inference-cost measurements in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: V1 generates transparent foregrounds sequentially using SD1.5/AnimateDiff, bounding-box-guided attention, the Layer-Customized Module, Harmony-Consistency Bridge, and post-harmonization. V2 replaces this procedure with joint temporal serialization of layer latents in Wan2.1-1.3B, LayerAdaLN, layer-aware cross-attention, and three-stage training with mask and compositing losses. Full-video, background, foreground, and mask outputs are generated jointly.

E1.justification: Coverage shifts from prescribed multi-object trajectories, including collisions, to text-conditioned joint layer generation. V2 introduces VidLayer for training and evaluation: approximately 50K clips and 4M frames constructed from VidGen-1M, LaSOT, MOSE, YouTube-VOS, and GOT-10k. Its diverse aligned video layers replace v1's custom trajectory suite and AnimalKingdom reference data; the original trajectory-control evaluation is not retained.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates MotionCtrl, Peekaboo, and Direct-a-Video against LayerT2V in Table 2 and supplementary comparisons. V2 replaces these external comparators with LayerFlow and also evaluates a Native Mask VAE variant in its quantitative comparison and user study (Tables 1–2). These are substantive comparator replacements.

E3.justification: V1 evaluates 256×256, 16-frame videos using FID/FVD, CLIPSIM, and trajectory metrics on 20 trajectory combinations with 10–12 prompt sets each. V2 introduces progressive training up to 384×672 and 41 frames, evaluates 200 held-out VidLayer prompts using VBench and ViCLIP, and assesses individual layers. Its redesigned user study uses 30 participants and 25 prompts with randomized presentation, versus 15 participants in v1.

E4.justification: V1's KFA, oriented attention-sharing, and HCB ablations, extensive-layer blending, transplantation examples, and base-model failure analyses are replaced. V2 tests 4D versus native 3D RoPE, Native Mask VAE versus VAE LoRA, and incremental LayerAdaLN/cross-attention additions (Section 5.3, Figure 6, Table 3). Its appendices add dataset filtering examples and computational-cost analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and aggregate user preferences without repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's larger user study changes the evaluation design but does not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The reported results are substantially replaced. V1 Table 2 reports LayerT2V mIoU 30.12 and AP50 16.62; these results disappear. V2 Table 1 reports new layer-specific scores, including BL aesthetic quality 0.5391 versus LayerFlow's 0.4895, and Table 2 reports preferences of 0.724, 0.768, and 0.668 across three criteria. These are results under new conditions, not directly comparable performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: V1's formalization of bounding-box attention guidance, attention sharing/isolation, and two-stage conditioning is replaced by definitions of serialized layer latents, layer-specific modulation, semantic attention routing, and staged flow-matching, compositing, and mask objectives (v2 Equations 3–12). This materially changes the mathematical formulation, although neither version supplies theorem-based guarantees.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on pioneering layered video synthesis to resolve colliding trajectories, with claimed mIoU/AP50 improvements. V2 instead claims unified generation of full videos and editable layers within one denoising process, introduces VidLayer as the first large-scale multi-layer video dataset, and emphasizes fidelity, temporal coherence, and cross-layer consistency. The original trajectory-control contribution and numerical headline claims are removed.

C2.justification: V1 explains foreground interference and discusses mismatched boxes, unstable same-depth interactions, and an outdated backbone. V2 instead explains layer-identity ambiguity, categorical versus positional conditioning, and pretrained mask priors. Appendices E–F discuss computational limits, scarce multi-foreground data, small-object segmentation failures, and inpainting leakage. Its stated model limit is inconsistent: Section 3.3 and Appendix E describe two foreground layers, while Section 5.1 and Appendix A claim three.

D1.justification: V1's guidance coefficients, inference schedule, harmonization instructions, and bounding-box examples are replaced by detailed staged training schedules, optimizer settings, LoRA ranks, loss weights, and hardware information. V2 also provides annotation/filtering prompts, acceptance thresholds, and measured inference time and memory (Appendices A–D). Release wording changes from available code in v1 to promised code/data in v2's introduction, although its conclusion describes the dataset as released.

R1.justification: The positioning moves from trajectory-control methods and attention manipulation to joint layered generation and modern video backbones. V2 identifies LayerFlow as the closest work and adds discussions of TransPixeler, TransAnimate, Wan-Alpha, StM, and Over++. LayerDiffuse remains cited, but the surrounding literature and claimed distinction from prior work are substantially reconstructed.

P1.justification: The title, author list, abstract, introduction, method exposition, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 adds a dedicated VidLayer section and reorganizes the supplementary material into implementation, computational cost, data construction, user study, visual samples, and limitations. This is a broad narrative and structural rewrite.

P2.justification: V1's sequential-generation diagrams, trajectory comparison tables, and component illustrations are replaced by joint-training and dataset diagrams, distribution charts, per-layer metric tables, and new visual comparisons. V2 also introduces boxed annotation prompts, a user-study interface, and predominantly single-column appendix text. These are extensive display and layout changes, beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V2 improves the assessability of its new framework through detailed training and data-construction recipes, resource measurements, and a randomized user-study protocol. However, it substantially redirects the research rather than establishing a comparable improvement over v1's trajectory-control approach. Its new evidence also has documentation problems: conflicting two-versus-three-foreground claims and fishing prompts attached to car and child examples in Figure 13. The reporting gains coexist with uncertainty about demonstrated scope and qualitative evidence, preventing a reliable net judgment of overall paper quality.
